results.q: What does the 2022 ADA settlement commit the MTA to, long term?
results.text:
Under the 2022 ADA settlement (CIDNY v. MTA, approved June 22, 2022), the MTA committed to a long-term, legally enforceable plan to maximize step-free access system-wide. Key long-term commitments:

**The big goal:** Make 95% of the 364 currently inaccessible subway stations step-free by 2055 [2022 ADA settlement (PDF)](/docs/mta-ada-settlement-2022.pdf).

**RFP milestones for at least 81 additional accessible stations (2020-2024 Capital Plan):**
- 25% of designated stations already had RFPs issued when the agreement was signed in 2022
- 60% by the end of 2023
- The remainder by the end of 2025 (subject to real estate/parkland issues)
[2022 ADA settlement (PDF)](/docs/mta-ada-settlement-2022.pdf)

**Further milestones beyond 2024** — the MTA must issue RFPs for:
- 85 more stations by 2035
- 90 more by 2045
- 90 more by 2055
(At least 75% of each milestone target must be met to be in compliance; targets scale down if construction costs inflate more than 150% from the 2020-2024 baseline.) [2022 ADA settlement (PDF)](/docs/mta-ada-settlement-2022.pdf)

**Funding guarantee:** For the 2020-2024 Capital Plan, if transit facilities funding hits $35.389B+, at least 14.69% must go to accessibility (with lower tiers down to 8% if funding is lower). Future capital plans (2025-2029+) assume a similar ~14.69% minimum baseline, adjusted if state-of-good-repair work dominates the plan. [2022 ADA settlement (PDF)](/docs/mta-ada-settlement-2022.pdf)

**Accountability:** The MTA must report to class counsel every six months on RFP/completion progress, funding, delays, station substitutions, and infeasibility findings — and explain in writing (with a catch-up plan) if it misses a milestone. A federal judge retains jurisdiction to resolve disputes, and the settlement stays enforceable until roughly a year after the accessibility work is substantially complete. [2022 ADA settlement (PDF)](/docs/mta-ada-settlement-2022.pdf)

results.q: Who is eligible for Access-A-Ride?
results.text:
Access-A-Ride (AAR) is paratransit for people whose disabilities prevent them from using public buses or subways. Eligibility comes in several categories, and the MTA determines yours through an application plus an in-person individualized assessment ([Apply or recertify for Access-A-Ride](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/access-a-ride/apply-or-recertify-for-access-a-ride)):

**Categories**
- **Full** – eligible for all trips
- **Temporary full** – all trips, for a limited time
- **Continual** – ongoing, no recertification, just an update form every 5 years
- **Conditional** – only under specific circumstances (see below)
- **Temporary conditional** – conditional, for a limited time
- **Ineligible** – doesn't meet criteria

**Conditional eligibility** applies when a disability only sometimes prevents fixed-route travel, e.g. ([Conditional Eligibility](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/access-a-ride/policies-and-forms/conditional-eligibility)):
- Only accessible option is an inaccessible subway station
- Extreme cold (≤39°F forecast) or extreme heat (≥90°F forecast)
- Distance conditions — e.g., eligible only when the nearest stop/station is more than 1–2, 3–4, or 5+ blocks away (your specific threshold is set individually)
- Unfamiliarity with routes due to cognitive/visual impairment (for unfamiliar routes only)

**How they decide:** review of your application, medical documentation, and an in-person assessment testing whether you can climb subway stairs, travel to a station/stop, board/ride/exit, and navigate the system independently — also evaluating gait, balance, endurance, strength, range of motion, and cognitive/psychological factors ([Eligibility Criteria](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/access-a-ride/policies-and-forms/eligibility-criteria)).

**Equal Access Policy:** multiple disabilities (even combined) can qualify you, and **episodic disabilities** (conditions that come and go) count if they prevent fixed-route use when active ([Conditional Eligibility](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/access-a-ride/policies-and-forms/conditional-eligibility)).

**Visitors:** if you're already paratransit-eligible in your home city/state, you can use AAR for up to 21 days per year — apply at least 2 weeks before arrival ([Apply or recertify for Access-A-Ride](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/access-a-ride/apply-or-recertify-for-access-a-ride)).

Decisions come within 21 days of your assessment; if denied or given conditional status, you have 60 days to appeal.

results.q: How do I report a broken elevator or get outage alerts?
results.text:
Here's how to check status, get alerts, and report a broken elevator:

**Check status before you travel**
- [Elevator/escalator status page](https://mta.info/elevator-escalator-status) — live outage info
- Call **511**, say "MTA," then "Subway and Buses," then "current service status," press 2. TTY/hearing-loss users can use 711 relay.

**Get outage alerts**
- [Sign up for email/text alerts](https://cloud.info.mta.org/create-mta-service-alerts?utm_source=accessibility&utm_medium=referral_link&utm_campaign=elevator_escalator_status_signup) on elevator/escalator service changes.

**Report a broken elevator (file an ADA complaint)**
- **Online:** [MTA feedback form](https://contact.mta.info/s/customer-feedback) — logs directly into their tracking system
- **Phone:** Call 511, ask to report an ADA issue
- **App:** Chat in the MTA app (subway/bus)
- **Mail:** addresses listed at mta.info/contact-us/regular-mail
- **Email ADA Coordinator:** NYCTADACoordinator@nyct.com (subway/bus) or accessibility@mtahq.org (general, will forward)

You'll get a case ticket number. Quick issues get routed within 1 business day; complex cases get a response within 15 business days.

(Source: [Accessible Travel by Subway](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/subway); [Make an ADA-related complaint or request](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/ada-complaint))

If you want, I can also check live status at a specific station right now — just tell me which one.

results.q: Am I eligible for a reduced fare if I have a disability?
results.text:
Yes — riders with qualifying disabilities can get a reduced fare, but the details differ by system, and my knowledge base only fully covers this for **commuter rail (LIRR & Metro-North)**, not the general subway/bus Reduced-Fare MetroCard/OMNY program specifically:

**LIRR & Metro-North reduced fare** (confirmed in my knowledge base):
- Riders with qualifying disabilities (and riders 65+) pay **half the one-way peak fare** [MTA Accessible travel by commuter rail](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/mta-railroads)
- Accepted ID: a Reduced-Fare OMNY Card/MetroCard, a paratransit card (Access-A-Ride, Able-Ride, or SCAT), a Medicare card (not Medicaid), or proof of age 65+
- Reduced fare **can't** be used on weekday morning peak trains arriving 6–10 a.m. at Penn Station, Grand Central, Atlantic Terminal, Hunterspoint Ave, or Long Island City — but it works fine in the evening peak

**Subway/bus reduced fare:** My knowledge base is scoped to accessibility topics and doesn't include the general subway/bus Reduced-Fare MetroCard/OMNY enrollment rules for people with disabilities — I don't want to guess at eligibility criteria I haven't actually verified. For that, please check directly at [mta.info/fares](https://www.mta.info/fares) or call 511.

Separately, note that **Access-A-Ride (AAR) eligibility** is a different thing — it's about qualifying for paratransit service (not a fare discount), based on whether your disability prevents you from using accessible buses/subways at all [Access-A-Ride Eligibility](https://www.mta.info/accessibility/access-a-ride/apply-or-recertify-for-access-a-ride). Let me know if you'd like details on that instead.
